prompt: Without end-user IDs, what does a provider see when one of Tarefa's users abuses the assistant?
hint: What does an API key identify?

choices.text: The account inside Tarefa that sent each request
choices.why: The provider has no way to know Tarefa's accounts unless Tarefa tells it.

choices.text: The user's IP address, which identifies the person to it
choices.why: The requests come from Tarefa's servers; the user's address never reaches the provider.

choices.text: A stream of bad requests from Tarefa's key
choices.why: Right: the key names the customer, and every user shares it.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because abuse detection needs an end-user ID to run
choices.why: Detection runs on the requests; what it lacks is somebody narrower than Tarefa to blame.

prompt: Which of these does an end-user ID make possible? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two places were named: the provider, and Tarefa.

choices.text: The provider pointing at one user instead of restricting the whole key
choices.why: Yes: that is the provider's half.

choices.text: Tarefa limiting and billing each user separately
choices.why: Yes: the identifier is what a limit per user counts by.

choices.text: Tarefa answering "who sent this?" from its own logs
choices.why: Yes: if every call recorded it, as lesson 21 recommends.

choices.text: The provider sending the end user's own data back to them on request
choices.why: The provider cannot name the person; requests for data go to Tarefa as controller.

prompt: In Anthropic's Messages API, the end user's identifier goes in `metadata.___`.
hint: Two words joined by an underscore.

prompt: Why does the lesson keep the end user's identifier in its own field rather than writing it into the prompt?

choices.text: Text inside a prompt is not billed, so the field costs nothing extra
choices.why: Every token of the prompt is billed; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Providers reject a prompt that has an identifier written into its text
choices.why: They do not; it would simply be in the wrong place.

choices.text: The field is encrypted by the provider and the prompt is not
choices.why: Both travel the same way; the difference is who reads them.

choices.text: The model reads the prompt; the provider's systems read the field
choices.why: Right: the model does not need to know who is asking, and the abuse checks do.

prompt: Why is the SHA-256 of an e-mail address a weak end-user ID?
hint: The hash cannot be run backwards. Does it need to be?

choices.text: SHA-256 has been broken and can be run backwards
choices.why: It has not; the attack never runs it backwards.

choices.text: Anybody can hash a list of likely addresses and compare
choices.why: Right: `guard reverse` found Marcos's address on the 257th guess.

choices.text: Two different addresses often produce the same hash
choices.why: Collisions are not the problem; guessing is.

choices.text: The hash changes each time the address is typed with capitals
choices.why: The lab lowercases first, and that would make it unstable rather than reversible.

prompt: After how many guesses did `guard reverse` find the address behind the plain hash?
What does the secret key in an HMAC add that a plain hash lacks?
hint: Try checking a guess without it.

choices.text: It makes the hash longer, so it takes too long to compute
choices.why: The length was cut to 20 characters; the key is what matters.

choices.text: It encrypts the identifier so that Tarefa can decrypt it later
choices.why: An HMAC is a hash; Tarefa recomputes it, and nobody decrypts it.

choices.text: Checking any guess needs the key, so a list is useless
choices.why: Right: the same dictionary found nothing.

choices.text: It changes the identifier on every call, so nothing can be linked
choices.why: It is stable on purpose; linking a user's calls is the point.

prompt: Tarefa sends the same account's requests to two providers. Why does the lab use a different key for each?
hint: Imagine both providers' records in one place.

choices.text: Providers reject identifiers that another provider has already seen
choices.why: They have no way to know; the reason is on Tarefa's side.

choices.text: One key would produce identifiers too long for the second provider
choices.why: The length is the same whatever the key.

choices.text: A key can only be used with one model at a time
choices.why: A key is just bytes; nothing ties it to a model.

choices.text: So the two sets of identifiers cannot be joined to each other
choices.why: Right: `ac-7Q2M` is `eu-fe47…` at one and `eu-4805…` at the other.

prompt: Tarefa rotates its HMAC key on a fixed schedule every month. What follows? Choose all that apply.
hint: The identifier is a function of the account and the key.

choices.text: Every user gets a new identifier each month
choices.why: Yes: change the key and every output changes.

choices.text: The provider's abuse history for a user is cut off at each rotation
choices.why: Yes: last month's identifier and this month's look like two people.

choices.text: Tarefa can no longer find which account sent last month's requests
choices.why: It can, if it kept last month's key or stored each identifier beside its account.

choices.text: The old identifiers become reversible with a dictionary
choices.why: Without the old key they are as opaque as before.

prompt: With only the key's limit of 60 a minute, how many requests did the five users who were not running a script lose between them?
hint: Add the refused column for every user except the script.

prompt: With only the key's limit, why did the script still get 97 requests through?
hint: Who arrives most often when the window reopens?

choices.text: The provider gives priority to the requests that arrive most often
choices.why: Nobody is given priority; the script simply arrives more.

choices.text: A shared limit refuses whoever arrives when full, and the script arrives most
choices.why: Right: a shared budget goes mostly to whoever asks most.

choices.text: The script's identifier was missing, so the limit did not apply to it
choices.why: Every request carried its identifier; the key's limit ignores it.

choices.text: Ninety-seven is the provider's allowance for any single end user
choices.why: The only limit in that run was 60 a minute on the whole key.

prompt: Why is the per-user limit set well below the key's limit?

choices.text: So no single user uses up the budget everybody shares
choices.why: Right: at 60 per user, one script could still fill the key.

choices.text: Providers require it to be at most a third of the key's limit
choices.why: No such rule; the third is Tarefa's choice.

choices.text: Because a lower limit makes each request cheaper
choices.why: Price per request does not depend on the limit.

choices.text: So that legitimate users are refused now and then, as a warning
choices.why: In the second run no legitimate user was refused at all.

prompt: A user sends ten requests a day, each with a whole contract pasted in. No request limit is ever reached, and the bill climbs. What does the lesson add?

choices.text: A lower request limit per user, such as five a day
choices.why: The requests are few; the tokens in each are the problem.

choices.text: Moderating each request before it is sent
choices.why: Pasting a contract is not abuse a moderation category would flag.

choices.text: A daily token budget per user, on the same identifier
choices.why: Right: a request limit bounds the rate, and a token budget bounds the bill.

choices.text: Removing the end-user ID so the provider bills Tarefa less
choices.why: The bill is per token whatever the identifier says.

prompt: A request refused by a rate limit gets the HTTP status code ___, with a Retry-After header.
Put the life of one request through Tarefa's assistant in order.
items: Compute the user's identifier with the HMAC key
Check the user's limit and token budget
Send the request to the provider with the identifier in its field
Log the call under the identifier, not the e-mail

prompt: Match each candidate end-user ID to what is wrong with it, or right.
hint: One description on the right fits none of them.

pairs.left: HMAC of the account id, one key per provider
pairs.right: Stable, opaque, and not joinable across providers

pairs.left: A random value made fresh on every call
pairs.right: Links no two calls, so nobody can be blamed

prompt: A provider writes that requests tagged `eu-e60a7d3c4b19f8e25d07` broke its policies. What lets Tarefa act within minutes?
hint: The identifier has to lead back to an account.

choices.text: Asking the provider which account the identifier belongs to
choices.why: The provider never knew Tarefa's accounts; that was the point.

choices.text: An indexed column of identifiers in Tarefa's own database
choices.why: Right: one lookup, instead of recomputing the identifier for every account.

choices.text: Reversing the identifier with a dictionary of Tarefa's e-mail addresses
choices.why: An HMAC does not reverse that way, and the input was an account id.

choices.text: Rotating the HMAC key so that the identifier stops working
choices.why: That changes every user's identifier and finds nobody.
